Guided Inquiry

Predict — a light block in water

An object of density 500 kg/m³ is placed in water (1000 kg/m³). How much of it sits below the waterline?

Watch it settle

Press ▶ Play. The block lowers into water. Watch the balance reading fall and the displaced-fluid weight rise by exactly the same amount — that equality IS Archimedes' principle. When the block floats, the balance reads zero: buoyancy took the whole load.

Read the fraction off the block

The waterline is drawn across the block. What fraction of it lies below?

Switch the fluid — now mercury

Same 500 kg/m³ block — now imagine the tank is mercury (13600 kg/m³). Before looking, what happens?

Push it under — then sink it

Keep the 500 kg/m³ block in water and drag Depth. Buoyancy grows as more volume goes under, then stops once the block is fully immersed.

Then set object density to 2700 (aluminium). The block SINKS: the balance reads apparent weight = true weight − buoyant force, and Depth no longer changes FB — the block is already fully under.

Ice at 917 kg/m³ in water → 91.7% submerged. That's why so little of an iceberg shows.

01

At a glance

A block hangs from a spring balance above a tank of fluid. You choose the density of the block and of the fluid, and the sim shows how the block sits in the tank and what the balance holds.

What you'll learn

  • How the fluid pushes up on a block placed in it, and how that push relates to what a spring balance reads.
  • How the part of a block that sits below the surface depends on the block and on the fluid.
  • How the push of the fluid changes when the block is held deeper.
The block starts above the surface on a spring balance. You set ρ and ρf.

What's on screen

  • Block and tank: the part of the block below the waterline is shaded teal and a label gives its percentage.
  • Balance reads (amber bar): the force the spring holds up, in newtons.
  • Displaced weight (teal bar): the weight of the fluid the block pushes aside.
  • Readouts (sidebar): Submerged fraction and Density ratio ρ/ρf.
See itOpen the sim with its opening values: a 500 kg/m³ block in a fluid of 1000 kg/m³. Watch for: the block sitting in the tank with a waterline across it, a percentage label, and a bar of each colour.

Fixed: the block always has volume V = 2.7 L (0.0027 m³) and g = 9.81 m/s², so its mass is m = ρV.

03

Buoyancy equals the weight of the fluid displaced

A block in a fluid pushes some fluid aside. The fluid pushes back with an upward buoyant force FB, equal to the weight of the fluid pushed aside.

FB = ρf Vdisp g
Vdisp is the volume of the block that is below the surface.

The spring balance holds up what the fluid does not. It reads the apparent weight Wapp = mg − FB, never below 0. For a block at rest, the two bars therefore add up to its true weight mg, the dashed line.

Take ρ = 2700 kg/m³ in water. The mass is 2700 × 0.0027 = 7.29 kg, so mg = 71.5 N. The block is fully under, so FB = 1000 × 0.0027 × 9.81 = 26.5 N, and the balance reads 71.5 − 26.5 = 45.0 N.

See itSet ρ = 2700 kg/m³ in water. Watch for: the bar labels 45.0 N (Balance reads) and 26.5 N (Displaced weight), which add up to the dashed true weight 71.5 N.
04

A floating block displaces exactly its own weight

A block with ρ ≤ ρf floats at rest. The fluid then carries the whole load, FB = mg, so the balance reads 0 N. With Vsub the volume below the surface:

ρf Vsub g = ρ V g  ⟹  Vsub / V = ρ / ρf
g cancels, and V cancels from the right-hand side.

The fraction of the block under the surface is the density ratio, which is why the sim's two readouts agree while the block floats. At ρ = ρf the block is just fully under.

For the opening values, 500 / 1000 = 0.500, and FB = mg = 1.35 × 9.81 = 13.2 N.

See itUse the opening values, ρ = 500 and ρf = 1000. Watch for: the label 50.0% under, both readouts at 0.500, the balance at 0.0 N and the displaced weight at 13.2 N.
05

In a denser fluid the same block sits higher

Changing only the fluid leaves the block's weight mg unchanged, and a floating block must still get FB = mg. A denser fluid supplies that force from less displaced volume, so Vsub = m / ρf falls as ρf rises. For the 500 kg/m³ block:

fluidρf (kg/m³)fraction under
oil-like8000.625
water10000.500
mercury136000.037

Even iron, at about 7870 kg/m³, floats in mercury with 7870 / 13600 = 58% of it under. The density ratio decides everything here, not the size or the weight of the block.

See itKeep ρ = 500 and set ρf = 13600 kg/m³. Watch for: the fluid labelled mercury and the block almost out of it, with the label 3.7% under.
06

A block denser than the fluid sinks, and the balance holds the rest

If ρ > ρf, the fluid cannot hold the block up: Vdisp can never exceed V, so FB tops out at ρf V g, which is less than mg. The block would sink if released, so the balance holds the difference.

Wapp = mg − ρf V g = (ρ − ρf) V g
Valid for ρ > ρf. The sim writes SINKS in red.

With ρ = 2700 and ρf = 2000 kg/m³: (2700 − 2000) × 0.0027 × 9.81 = 18.5 N. Whether a block floats depends on the pair of densities. The same 2700 block floats in mercury, with 2700 / 13600 = 19.9% of it under.

See itSet ρ = 2700 and ρf = 2000 kg/m³. Watch for: the red SINKS note, the Balance reads bar at 18.5 N and the Displaced weight bar at 53.0 N.
07

Pushing a block deeper adds buoyancy only until it is fully under

The Depth pushed under slider forces a floating block below its resting level. More of the block is then below the surface, so Vdisp and FB rise, until the block is fully under at 1.00. After that nothing more is displaced and FB = ρf V g stays fixed. A block that sinks starts fully under, so this slider changes nothing for it.

Depth, ρ = 500 in waterfraction underFB
0.000.50013.2 N
0.500.75019.9 N
1.001.00026.5 N

Holding a floating block under needs an extra downward force of FB − mg from outside, 13.2 N at 1.00. The sim draws only FB.

Go deeper: why FB = ρf V g

Take a block of height h and flat face area A, with its top face a depth d below the surface. The pressure there is ρf g d, and at the bottom face ρf g (d + h). The net upward force is ρf g h A = ρf g V, and d cancels.

See itKeep ρ = 500 in water and push the Depth slider to 1.00. Watch for: Submerged fraction at 1.000 while Density ratio stays at 0.500, and the Displaced weight bar at 26.5 N, double the 13.2 N it showed at rest.
08

Where it matters

  • Ships. Steel is much denser than water, but a hull encloses a lot of air. The ship's average density is below the water's, so it floats and displaces its own weight of water.
  • Icebergs. Ice is about 917 kg/m³. In fresh water 91.7% of it is under, and in sea water (about 1025 kg/m³) about 89%. Most of an iceberg is out of sight.
  • Hydrometers. A weighted tube floats until it displaces its own weight of liquid. In a denser liquid it floats higher, so the level on the tube reads density.
  • Weighing for density. Weigh a solid in air and again in water. The loss is FB, which gives the solid's volume, and so its density. This is how Archimedes could test a crown.
09

Summary

In one line. This sim compares a block's density with a fluid's density to decide how the block sits in the fluid and what the spring balance holds.

Key points

  • FB = ρf Vdisp g, and the balance reads Wapp = mg − FB.
  • A floating block has Vsub / V = ρ / ρf, and the balance reads 0.
  • A block with ρ > ρf is held by the balance with (ρ − ρf) V g.

Common mix-ups

  • "Heavy things sink and light things float." Density against the fluid decides it. A steel ship floats and a nail sinks.
  • "The fluid pushes up with the block's weight." Only a floating block at rest gets FB = mg. A sinking block gets less.
  • "Deeper means more buoyancy." Only until the block is fully under. After that FB no longer changes with depth.

Things to try on your own

  • Find the fluid density at which the 500 kg/m³ block is just fully under, and read both readouts there.
  • Predict the balance reading for ρ = 4000 in water, then check it.
  • Set ρ = 2700 and raise ρf until the red SINKS note disappears. Read ρf there.
